name: Jita
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Jita (jita1239) is not in the catalog. The two title-hit items are Philippson's 1991 Paris 5 thesis on tone and accent in East African Bantu (comparative; Glottolog codes Jita among ~30 languages; theses.fr record saved, 'accessible: non', abstract only: a continuum from pure tone to demarcative penultimate stress, with penultimate accent as the diachronic driver) and Downing's 1995 LINCOM chapter on the metrical domain of register raising in Jita (OT tone/metrical-domain analysis; no online copy anywhere checked: ROA, archive.org, Open Library, ORCID, gup.ub.gu.se, HathiTrust/Google Books blocked). Both remain unread; both are medium-priority print acquisitions (Downing 1995 the more Jita-specific; Philippson 1991 more likely to give a one-line prosodic-type classification of Jita). All readable first-hand Jita sources already on file from the earlier audit (Downing 1988, 2014; Kagaya 2003 abstract, 2005; SIL 2016 orthography statement and grammar basics) are tone descriptions silent on word stress; Downing 2004 leaves Jita out of her Bantu stress-accent table and only reports Kenstowicz 1993's stress-analogy for Jita H tone. No first-hand stress statement found; best_new_statement = none. Google, Bing, Brave, DuckDuckGo blocked from our machine) limited discovery to API/repository fetches

sources.citation: Odom, Shannon Ronit & Holly Robinson. 2016. The Grammar Basics of Jita. Dallas: SIL International (Uganda-Tanzania Branch). 24 pp.
sources.note: Morphosyntax sketch; only a one-page orthography note (5 vowels, 17 consonants, contrastive and conditioned vowel length). Tone not marked; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 2005. A Jita Vocabulary. Asian and African Lexicon 47. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. xxi+482 pp. DOI 10.15026/81524.
sources.note: Mrangi (northern) dialect. Outline of Grammar §1 Phonemes (PDF p. 10): short/long vowels; 'A vowel before a prenasalized consonant /NC/ tends to be long. Especially, it is definitely long when the vowel before a prenasalized consonant is placed on the penultimate syllable of a word.' §4 Tone (PDF pp. 12-13): two level tones L and H, F/R on long syllables, four noun tone types. No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 1988. Tonology of noun-modifier phrases in Jita. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 18(1): 25-60.
sources.note: Noun tone patterns and phrasal H insertion; p. 27: 'Using a non-accentual approach, I analyze these tone patterns as resulting from a rule of Noun Phrase High Insertion'; p. 28: 'Jita only has high tones underlyingly'. Nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Rolle, Nicholas R. 2018. Grammatical Tone: Typology and Theory. PhD dissertation, UC Berkeley.
sources.note: Uses Jita melodic-tone data from Downing 1996/2014 at several points; no statement about Jita stress.

sources.citation: Odom, Shannon Ronit (author; from Kiraka & Nicholls' sketch). 2016. Jita Orthography Statement: Approved Orthography Edition. SIL International, Uganda-Tanzania Branch. 55 pp.
sources.note: §2 Phonology: vowels, contrastive length, conditioned length before NC and after Cy/Cw, consonants; §2.3 Tone: active lexical and grammatical tone, few minimal pairs, tone unwritten except colon for Distant Past. No mention of stress, accent or penultimate lengthening.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2014. Melodic verb tone patterns in Jita. Africana Linguistica 20: 101-119. DOI 10.3406/aflin.2014.1026.
sources.note: Tone-only description (H/L verb stems, OCP deletion, one-syllable rightward H shift except phrase-penult/final, melodic H patterns); data from one Ukerewe-island consultant. No mention of stress, accent or penultimate lengthening (grep of full scanned text).

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2004. What African languages tell us about accent typology. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 37: 101-136.
sources.note: Secondary survey by the primary describer. p. 102: Jita (Downing 1996) cited among languages 'described as accentual or non-tonal by earlier scholars which are currently accepted as having tone'. Jita is absent from Table (15) 'Summary table of stress-accent in Bantu languages' (pp. 121-122). pp. 125-128 treat Jita H-tone culminativity, Meeussen's Rule and tone shift as pitch-accent-like properties; p. 128: 'Kenstowicz (1993) argues that delinking is best explained if High tone in Jita is analogous to stress accent.' No statement of a word-stress position.

From the title and Downing's other Jita work on file (1988 SLS article, 1996 monograph as cited in Downing 2004 and 2014, 2014 Africana Linguistica), this is an OT analysis of the metrical (prosodic-domain) conditioning of a tonal register-raising process in Jita's H-tone system, i.e. tone/metrical-domain phonology, not a word-stress placement statement.
